activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
story:
The smell hit Savannah before she reached the door: braised pork, star anise, something sweet and scorched from the kitchen where her grandmother was already shouting measurements at her father. It was Lunar New Year at her aunt's house, the same crowded rooms every year, the same plastic folding tables dragged up from the basement, the same arguments about whether the dumplings were folded correctly. Savannah stood in the hallway holding her gift bag of mandarin oranges and did the arithmetic she'd been doing since December. Eighteen in May. College in September. This was, by any honest count, her last New Year as a kid.

Her cousin's wife found her there, coat still on, and pressed a small rectangle into her palm before Savannah could get a word out. Red paper, crisp, the gold characters stamped slightly off-centre. "Hongbao," her cousin's wife said. "From us. For luck." Savannah closed her fingers around it and felt the strange weight of it, lighter than a phone, heavier somehow than the twenty dollars it probably held.

She found Seerat and Jazmine in the den, where the teenagers traditionally hid, eating fried wontons off a paper towel balanced on the arm of a chair. Seerat's family celebrated this too, though differently, in a house that smelled of cardamom instead of star anise, and Jazmine had come as she came every year, an honorary cousin by fourth grade. "Did you get yours yet?" Seerat asked, and Savannah held up the envelope. Jazmine frowned at it. "Wait, they give these to you? You're basically an adult. You vote in like seven months."

"Unmarried younger relatives still count," Savannah said. "That's the rule. It goes to kids and unmarried younger relatives." She'd learned it the way she learned most family rules, by watching, by being handed things without explanation, by the year her uncle forgot and her grandmother corrected him in two languages at once.

The problem arrived with her grandfather, who was ninety and precise and loved her in a way that sometimes felt like an audit. He came into the den for his tea, saw the envelope in her hand, and studied her the way he studied a chessboard. "Going away in the fall," he said. Not a question. "Big school, far away." Savannah said yes, and he nodded slowly, and she understood that in his ledger she was already crossing some line, that the envelopes and the childhood they implied might not find her next year, and that a part of her, a part she didn't want to extenuate or excuse, wanted them anyway. Wanted the red paper and the luck and the being claimed.

She thought about it through dinner, through the fish her father pointedly left half uneaten so there would be leftovers for the year ahead, through her grandmother's story about a beast called Nian, some malevolent thing that terrorized a village once, driven off by the colour red. So the envelopes were not just money. Red was good fortune; red warded off evil. That was the whole logic of it, though it wasn't logos exactly, not the clean syllogism she'd been drilling for debate class. It was older than argument. You could not prove a colour protected you. You could only accept the envelope.

After dinner she found her grandfather alone at the card table, tea gone cold beside him. She sat down across from him, and before she could decide what she wanted to say, he slid an envelope across the felt. "Last one, maybe," he said. "Or not. You come home, you get one. That is up to you." He said it gruffly, looking at the cards, but he left his hand flat on the table a moment longer than necessary.

Savannah picked up the envelope and held it in both hands. She didn't know yet whether she would come home for New Year from a city eight hundred miles away, whether she'd have money for the flight, whether college would make her too busy or too new a person for folding tables and folded dumplings. What she knew was smaller and enough for now: she was still, this year, in the circle the red paper marked out, and she could carry that with her without pretending it settled anything. "I'll come home," she said, and meant it as far as she could see.

Seerat appeared in the doorway with wontons and a demand for the card game to start, and Savannah slid the envelope into the inner pocket of her coat, red against her ribs, and dealt her grandfather in.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Using 2007 survey data, the US Census Bureau estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime.
story:
The moving truck smelled of cardboard and someone else's lavender air freshener, and Emily sat wedged between a rolled rug and a box labeled KITCHEN, MISC, because the cab only had two seats. Her mother drove. Somewhere behind them, in a different sense entirely, were Aurelia and Mitchell, who had promised to text and had, so far, texted.

"Did you know," her mother said, not taking her eyes off the highway, "that using 2007 survey data, the US Census Bureau estimated that a person in the United States can expect to move about 11.7 times in a lifetime?" She said it the way she said most statistics, as if reciting a spell against sadness. "Eleven point seven. You've done three."

"Great," Emily said. "Eight and a half to go."

"It's not nothing, is what I mean. People do this all the time. You're not being exiled."

Emily did not answer, because the truest response, that other people's suffering was a cold kind of comfort, would have started a conversation, and she wanted to watch the trees instead. Aurelia had cried at the goodbye, real tears, which Emily had found both touching and vaguely performative; Mitchell had not cried, had only said "this isn't a funeral, you'll be back at Thanksgiving," which was either the kindest or the cruelest thing anyone had said to her, and she had been turning it over for two hundred miles without deciding.

The new school had a smell, like all schools, of floor wax and disinfectant, but a different brand. Emily found her homeroom, then her locker, which stuck, then her first class: American Government with Ms. Pérez, a woman with gray-streaked hair and a coffee mug that said OBJECTION. On the board was a question: Is precedent a form of wisdom or a form of cowardice?

"Jurisprudence," Ms. Pérez said, pacing, "is supposed to be the answer to that question. The philosophy of law. How judges decide what to follow." She pointed the mug at a boy near the window. "Marcus, weigh in."

Marcus said precedent was wisdom, because if every judge started from scratch the law would be chaos. A girl in the front row said it was cowardice dressed up, a way to valorize the past just because it was the past, to treat old decisions as if age made them right. Emily, who in her old school had been the one who talked, wrote both arguments in her notebook and noticed something: each one could be turned against itself. If you respected precedent because it was stable, you could justify anything stable. If you distrusted it because it was old, you were just valorizing the new. The reasoning on both sides struck her as tautological, each conclusion already hiding inside its premise, and she raised her hand before she fully meant to.

"You're saying the same thing from opposite ends," she said, when Ms. Pérez called on her. "One side says old equals trustworthy, the other says new equals trustworthy. Neither one's actually looking at whether the decision was good."

The room went quiet in the way rooms do when a stranger says something that lands. Ms. Pérez tilted her head. "And how would you decide if a decision was good?"

"I don't know yet," Emily said. "Maybe you can't, entirely. Maybe you weigh it each time, and it's slow, and nobody gets to be certain."

"Then you'd better get comfortable with slow," Ms. Pérez said, but she was almost smiling. "Sit with that. We'll come back to you."

At lunch Emily sat alone, which she had rehearsed for and which was still worse than rehearsed. Aurelia had sent a photo of the old lunch table with a space left open, caption: your seat, held. Mitchell had sent nothing since morning, which stung differently. She ate half a sandwich and thought about the eleven point seven, the number riding in her head all day like a passenger. Her mother had offered it as proof that moving was ordinary, survivable, a thing people simply did. But standing in a cafeteria full of strangers, Emily found the number could be read the other way too: if she would likely do this many more times, then this town, these people, this whole painstaking beginning was provisional. Why spend herself on it?

Except that the alternative, holding back until she landed somewhere permanent, had a flaw she couldn't get around, because eleven point seven was an average, not a schedule, and there was no final address waiting for her at the end. There was only the series of places. If she waited to belong until belonging was guaranteed, she would be doing the cowardice thing, not the wisdom thing, and she would have dressed it up as prudence.

In sixth period a girl with a lanyard full of enamel pins appeared at her elbow and asked if she wanted to be on the trivia team, because they were short a person and Emily had said that thing in government class, and word traveled even in a school she'd occupied for six hours. Emily said she didn't know anything about trivia. The girl said nobody did, that was the point, and held out a sign-up sheet with a pen.

Emily looked at the blank line for her name, thought of Aurelia holding her seat open six hundred miles away, and wrote.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The ocean stores heat from summer and releases it into the air in winter, and prevailing westerly winds carry that warmth onto northwestern Europe.
story:
The chart had come down from the attic folded into quarters, and Maelle spread it across her grandfather's kitchen table, weighting the corners with his teacup, a jar of marmalade and two smooth grey stones from the beach below the house. It was an old ocean current map of the North Atlantic, printed in faded blues and arrows, and across it in red ink someone had once traced the Gulf Stream's long reach toward the frozen-looking upper corner of the map. Her presentation was on Thursday. She had promised Ms. Clarke she could stand up in front of the class and explain, in plain words, why Britain and Norway sat at the same latitude as Labrador yet enjoyed winters Labrador would not recognise.

"So which is it," Bastien asked from the doorway, shaking rain off his jacket. "Does the current warm the land directly, like a radiator under a window, or is there a trick to it?" He and Harleen had taken two buses out from town because Maelle had texted that the house was quiet and the map was enormous and she was, in her own words, drowning.

"There's a trick," Harleen said, pulling out a chair. "There has to be. If it were just the water touching the coast, only the coast would be warm. But the whole of northwestern Europe is mild. Ireland barely sees snow." She traced the Atlantic with one finger, from the Caribbean northeastward. "The heat travels somewhere after the sea."

Maelle leaned over the table, frowning at the arrows. "The ocean stores heat from summer," she said slowly, reading off her own notes, then stopping, because the next part she did not yet believe. "And it releases it into the air in winter. That part I keep almost saying and then not saying, because I can't picture it. How does a sea hold anything?"

Her grandfather came in with the teapot and stood behind her for a moment without speaking, the way he did when he wanted her to find the answer rather than be handed it. He refilled his cup, then hers, then slid the marmalade a safe distance from the chart's edge where it had begun to wrinkle the paper.

"Think of August," he said. "You swim here in August and the water holds the sun a month after the beaches empty. It doesn't give it up all at once." Then he went back to his chair by the window and said nothing more, which was his way of teaching.

Bastien was chewing the end of a pencil. "Fine, so in winter the sea is letting go of summer. Warm air comes up off the water. But Britain is not sitting in the water. Norway is hardly touching it. So the warmth has to be carried." He looked at the map's margin, where small feathered symbols marked wind. "Which way do the winds go? That's the whole question. Harleen asked me this on the bus and I said it didn't matter and she said it mattered more than anything."

"Wind direction matters," Maelle said, mostly to herself, and then she saw it. The feathers on the chart blew east, from the Atlantic onto the land, west to east, and she put her finger on them and followed her own finger with her eyes across Ireland, across Britain, across the low countries and up toward Scandinavia. "The prevailing westerly winds. They come from the west. They pick up the air the ocean has warmed and carry it onto northwestern Europe. That's why it's not just the ports that are mild, it's everything downwind." She stood back from the table. "It's not a radiator under the window. It's the wind delivering the heat inland, like mail."

Harleen made her say it twice more, once without looking at the map, and then set about testing her the way she tested everything, playing the hostile examiner. "I impugn your arrows," she announced, tapping the faded print. "This map is older than Maelle. Why should I trust winds that were blowing before either of us could read?" Maelle laughed and pulled up the modern current data on her phone, holding it beside the chart, and the arrows matched, decade over decade, and Harleen conceded with a small formal bow.

Bastien, meanwhile, had wandered to the bookshelf and found an old folder of her grandfather's papers, among them a sworn statement from a dispute over the boundary of the neighbouring field, decades old, signed and stamped. "Look, an affidavit," he said. "Your grandfather put his name to a fact and made it stick." Maelle took it from him, turned it over in her hands, and understood suddenly what she wanted on Thursday: not to recite, but to speak as though she had signed something. She looked out the window at the grey Atlantic rolling in below the house, the same water on the chart, and thought of it in January, when the beaches were empty and the air above it would be holding the last of a summer nobody remembered, generous and unremarked, nothing malevolent in it at all.

On Thursday morning Ms. Clarke called her to the front. Maelle unrolled a photocopy of the chart, weighted the corners with four whiteboard markers, and asked the class to find Britain with their eyes, then look west, out to sea, and wait.

"Now," she said, "tell me which way the wind is blowing."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Ford Madox Ford's 1915 novel The Good Soldier opens with its narrator, John Dowell, saying, 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard.'
story:
Nolan's grandmother kept her television in a cabinet with doors, as though the news were something to be shut away between meals, and this was where he sat with The Good Soldier open on his knee, trying to finish it before Monday. The assignment from Ms. Addo was due in five days, and it required something more than a summary. Trust, she had said, was the reader's currency, and the essay was supposed to examine how a narrator spends it. Nolan had read the first page four times and copied the opening line onto a napkin at lunch, where Bryden had leaned over and asked if he was writing a suicide note.

"This is the saddest story I have ever heard," Nolan read aloud to the empty room. His grandmother was in the kitchen making something with onions that she claimed was a stew and that Nolan suspected was a strategy for keeping him at the table. He said the sentence again, slower. The narrator, John Dowell, had lived the whole thing, married to the woman at the center of it, present for nine years of what happened. And yet he called it a story he had heard, as if he had been sitting in a club chair while somebody else told it to him.

Bryden came over after his shift at the garden center, still smelling of fertilizer, and wanted exactly one thing, which was to hijack Nolan's laptop long enough to watch a match replay that had already ended. "I know the score," Bryden admitted, dropping onto the couch. "That's not the point. I want to see the goals happen." He had a whole theory about this, something about how knowing the outcome made the goals purer. He set up the replay with the insouciant air of a man who believed that wanting something was enough to underwrite getting it, and Nolan let him, because Bryden had driven him to the dentist in March and had never once mentioned it.

While the match murmured in the background, Nolan thought about a Tuesday three weeks earlier, before school had let out for the summer. Ms. Addo had stood at the whiteboard with her marker uncapped and asked the class who, in a courtroom, decided whether a witness was telling the truth. Hayden had said the jury, and she had said no, the jury decides what to believe; the lawyers decide what to make you believe, and a subpoena can drag a witness into the room but cannot make him reliable. Then she had assigned the novel and said nothing else, which at the time had seemed like laziness and now seemed like a trap.

"You're frowning at a book," Bryden said during halftime, which did not exist in a replay but which Bryden observed anyway, out of principle. Nolan turned the book around and showed him the first line. "Ford Madox Ford, 1915," Nolan said. "It opens with the narrator saying, 'This is the saddest story I have ever heard.' But it's his own life. His wife, his friends, all of it happened to him." Bryden chewed on this while a goal he already knew about happened on the screen behind him. "So he's lying," Bryden said. "Or he's stupid." Nolan said he didn't think it was either, exactly, and Bryden said that was the kind of answer that got you a C, and went back to his match.

The problem kept its shape all through dinner. Nolan's grandmother ladled the stew and asked about school, and he told her about the essay, and she said that her late husband had told the story of how they met in four different versions over forty years and that she had liked the third one best, where he claimed to have rescued her hat from the sea. She had never owned such a hat. She said this without bitterness, the way you might report the weather from a decade ago. Nolan asked which version was true, and she said that a man who loved you would tell you a story worth hearing, and that the truth was whatever he could not stop changing.

That night, at the small desk in the guest room, under a lamp with a shade the color of weak tea, Nolan wrote the sentence that Ms. Addo would later read twice and underline in green. He wrote that Dowell calls the story one he heard because hearing it is safer than living it, and that Ford had built the whole novel on that single word, heard, so that the reader spends four hundred pages deciding whether to pity the man or suspect him. Then he wrote a second sentence admitting that he could not prove Dowell was lying, only that a narrator who hands you his own life as gossip has already taught you how to doubt him. He looked at both sentences for a long time. In the other room, faintly, he could hear his grandmother telling the phone, presumably, the version with the hat.

Bryden texted at eleven, a single question about whether the replay's final goal had been offside, followed by an argument Nolan could not adjudicate from the guest room. He set the phone face-down, and the book still open beside his notebook, and turned off the lamp. In the dark the desk kept the shape of unfinished work, the essay's last line unwritten, and through the wall his grandmother's voice went on, unhurried, rescuing the hat from the sea again.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The dependency ratio compares people aged under 15 and 65 and over with people aged 15 to 64, estimating how many dependents each working-age person supports.
story:
Rosalie told everyone the summer at her grandmother's house was a vacation, which was true the way a photograph of a house is true. She had her textbook, her notes from Mr. Chaudhry's last unit, and a phone that buzzed most evenings with Sage asking whether she'd started the practice questions yet. She said she had, most nights, and mostly she hadn't. Grandmother was fine, she told her mother on the phone. Grandmother was doing great.

The assignment was a population pyramid: bars for every age group, men on one side, women on the other, and the question underneath, which Mr. Chaudhry had underlined twice. Decide whether this country should build more schools or more nursing homes, and defend it. Rosalie liked questions with one right answer, and this was not one of those, which was why she kept not starting it.

She started it at the kitchen table because the kitchen had the best light and Grandmother liked company without admitting it. Grandmother sat across from her shelling peas, listening to the radio, occasionally asking what all the little bars meant. Rosalie drew the pyramid for a country whose base was narrow and whose middle bulged, then one whose base spread wide and shallow, and slid them across the table. "They're called population pyramids," she said, which was obvious, but Grandmother nodded as though it weren't.

The peas went into a bowl. Grandmother put on her glasses and studied the wide-based one. "So this one is a young country," she said, tapping the bottom bars. "Lots of children. This one is like us." She tapped the other sheet, the one that looked like a top-heavy Christmas tree. "Not enough young people coming up underneath." That much Rosalie had already gotten from the book, though hearing it said plainly in the warm kitchen made it feel newly real, the way a place you've seen in photographs feels real only when you stand in it.

The part she kept rereading was the phrase in her notes, dependency ratio, and the sentence under it, which compared people aged under 15 and 65 and over with people aged 15 to 64, estimating how many dependents each working-age person supports. She said the phrase aloud to try to make it stick, and Grandmother asked what it meant, and Rosalie found she could say it: the people too young or too old to work, set against the people in between, and how many of the first group each person in the second group has to carry. Grandmother was quiet for a moment, then laughed, a short dry sound. "So that's me," she said. "I'm one of the numbers on the wrong side of your little bars."

Rosalie said, correctly, that Grandmother had worked for forty years and had earned her place, and Grandmother waved this off, but she kept looking at the pyramid, at the tall thin bars near the top where her own age group lived, the bars that were longer now than they had been in the old charts in the book. Rosalie's mother called while they were sitting there, and after, Rosalie tried out the argument on her, the one she was building for the assignment. An aging population means each working-age person supports more dependents, so taxes on workers go up, or services get cut, or both. Her mother made a noncommittal sound that Rosalie ascribed to the bad signal, though later she wondered if it was something else, the sound of a person doing arithmetic about her own mother.

Rowan texted a photo of his finished assignment, annotated, immaculate, and Rosalie felt the familiar dull pressure of being behind. She worked through the evening while Grandmother watched a quiz show. She had been thinking of the pyramid as a picture of strangers, some country she'd never visit, but the shapes kept resolving into this kitchen. Wide base, many mouths, many schools. Narrow base, tall top, nursing homes, and the workers in the middle squeezed thinner and thinner, and one of those workers her mother, and one of those dependents two feet away shouting the answer at the television before the contestant could.

She wrote her answer in two paragraphs, which felt like a compromise and also like the truth: the country needed the schools eventually, but the nursing homes first, because the tall bars were already here and the wide ones were still only projected. She acknowledged what she couldn't know, whether migration or birth rates would shift the bars before the buildings went up, whether the projection itself was a guess dressed as a fact. Sage read the draft over video call and said it was good, actually good, better than Rowan's neat one, and Rosalie believed her and also didn't, entirely.

On her last morning, Grandmother pressed a jar of the shelled peas into her bag, frozen, wrapped in a dish towel, and said she'd taught her something after all, hadn't she, without meaning to. Rosalie said yes, though what she was thinking was that it had been mutualism, the two of them feeding each other something, and that this was exactly the kind of sentence she'd have to stop writing now that college was starting. In the car her mother asked if she'd noticed anything, anything at all, about Grandmother, and Rosalie, watching the house shrink in the side mirror, said, "Like what?"

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In a time signature, the top number gives the number of beats in each bar and the bottom number gives the note value that gets one beat, so 4/4 means four quarter-note beats.
story:
The community centre smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Mr. Liu's music room at the end of the hall had one window that faced a parking lot instead of anything green, though Joshua liked to imagine the cracked asphalt as a savanna, yellow grass waiting somewhere under all that concrete. He had four Thursdays to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes, written out in standard notation, for the centre's spring showcase. He had never written a note down in his life.

His problem was simple and embarrassing. The tune in his head was long, flowing, profligate with notes, and every time he tried to trap it on paper it slipped into shapes that didn't add up. He'd write a bar he loved, then a second bar, and by the third something had drifted. Mr. Liu had refused to fix it for him. "You'll learn more from your own errors," he said, sliding the manuscript paper across the table, "but I won't litigate your bar lines for you. Counting is the composer's job, not mine."

Emelia sat across from him with a practice pad between her knees, tapping paradiddles with two pencils because her mother wouldn't pay for drumsticks until she "proved she was serious." She wanted the drumline spot at their school more than she had ever wanted anything, and she came to the centre on Thursdays even though it was a composition class, because Mr. Liu let her use the room's old metronome. She watched Joshua count on his fingers and frown.

"How's it going, Mozart?"

"Bad." He turned the paper toward her. In the first bar he had written a quarter note, two eighths, a half note, and then, because the melody needed one more step before it could turn around, another quarter. He'd done the same thing three bars later. "I like how it sounds. But when I play it against Emelia's metronome it lurches."

Emelia leaned over the page. She tapped her pencil along his notes, and her frown deepened with each bar. "Okay, so what time signature is this in?"

"Four-four. Obviously."

"Count the first bar, then."

He counted. Quarter, one. Two eighths, two. Half note, three, four. Then the last quarter, sitting there after the four like a guest who arrived after the table was cleared. Five beats. He counted the fourth bar and it was the same. He counted every bar, and half of them spilled over, and he sat back in the plastic chair.

"So the top number gives the number of beats in each bar," Emelia said, reading off the worn poster above the piano, "and the bottom number gives the note value that gets one beat. Four-four means four quarter-note beats." She tapped her pencil on his runaway bar. "You've got five in here. Twice."

He stared at the bar. He had two choices, and he could see them both clearly. He could cut the extra notes, which would make the melody obedient and shorter and would kill the loping, uneven drag that he actually loved, the thing that made it sound like something walking instead of marching. Or he could change the time signature, write five as the top number, and let the whole piece lean. He had read just enough to know that five-four existed. He hadn't known, until this moment, why anyone would choose it.

"Five," he said. "It's in five."

"That's weird," Emelia said, but she was already tapping it, five clicks to the bar, and when he played his melody over her pencil rhythm it stopped lurching and started breathing. Her own problem sat next to his on the table: the audition piece for drumline was in a fast three, and she'd been practicing it in four for two weeks because she'd never learned to read the numbers either. She took out a fresh sheet and copied the poster's fractions down the margin, one through eight, testing each against her hands.

Mr. Liu came over near the end of the hour and looked at the page for a long time. He hummed the first eight bars, then stopped. "Where did you hear this?" he asked.

"I didn't. I made it up."

Mr. Liu tapped the second bar, the one with the turn Joshua was proudest of. "My father hummed something like this. He worked on the railway, and he'd sing on the walks home. I haven't heard it in thirty years." He set the paper down. "Yours is in five. His was in four. So it isn't the same tune, whatever it is." He went back to the piano, and Joshua couldn't tell whether the man was dismissing the resemblance or mourning it.

Joshua rewrote all sixteen bars that night at the centre's upright piano, the radiator ticking beside his knee, Emelia still tapping in the corner with her metronome set to three. The melody was truer now, but shorter than the one in his head, and he'd had to give up two phrases he liked to make the chord changes sit right under the strange lopsided pulse. On the last page he wrote five over four at the beginning, then stopped, then wrote it again at the start of the section where the rhythm changed, because he still wasn't sure whether the piece wanted that or whether he was forcing it. He left both time signatures standing. Emelia looked over his shoulder and tapped her pencil twice against the paper's edge.

"You don't know if it's right," she said.

"No," Joshua said, and played the bar again.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Beyond the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, the Gulf Stream's continuation toward Europe is called the North Atlantic Current or North Atlantic Drift.
story:
The science museum kept its ocean room at a cool sixty-eight degrees, and Loic had memorized the number because Ms. Das said it every time she unlocked the doors for the student volunteers. He had taken the Saturday shift for the practical reason that it paid a stipend toward his deposit for college, and for the less practical reason that the North Atlantic wall map had begun to occupy his mind the way a song does, returning at odd hours, demanding to be understood. He stood before it now with Ty, who was supposed to be his partner on the floor and was instead leaning against the tsunami exhibit eating pretzels from his jacket pocket.

The problem was concrete: at one o'clock, a group of middle schoolers would arrive, and Loic had promised Ms. Das he could explain why Britain and Norway are warmer than their latitude deserves. He understood the premise. Warm water leaves the Gulf of Mexico, rides the American coast north, and carries heat across the ocean like a slow, enormous hand laid on Europe's shoulder. But the map kept breaking his sentence in half.

"Look at this," he said, and Ty came over, brushing salt from his fingers. The map's red ribbon of current swept up the eastern seaboard, widened past the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, and then, apparently, ceased. On the far side of that invisible line, a separate ribbon began, paler, fanning toward Ireland and Norway, labeled in a smaller font. Loic traced both with his finger. "Why does it change its name out there? Is it a different current? Did the Gulf Stream just stop?"

Ty suggested, reasonably, that the map was badly drawn. Loic wanted that to be true, because a badly drawn map could be dismissed, but he had spent enough evenings with the museum's reference shelf to know that maps were rarely accused of anything they hadn't done on purpose. He smelled the room's faint ozone-and-floor-wax air and felt the particular frustration that is almost pleasant, the kind that precedes figuring something out.

He found Rehan by the touch tank, sleeves rolled, letting a hermit crab examine his knuckle. Rehan had applied to three colleges for marine science and had opinions about everything wet. "The current doesn't stop," Rehan said when Loic described the map. "It gets a new name. Past the Grand Banks, its continuation toward Europe is called the North Atlantic Current. Some books say North Atlantic Drift, same thing." Loic felt something shift in him, less like learning a fact than like being handed the missing hinge of a door. The water kept flowing; only the word changed. Which raised a question he liked too much to keep to himself: was the name part of the water, or only part of the map?

He turned that over while he arranged the cart of laminated cards for the middle schoolers, and it exhilarated him in a way he couldn't quite justify to Ty, who pointed out that it was just a label. "But that's the point," Loic said. "The ocean doesn't have a customs office. The water doesn't know it crossed a line. We draw the line." He was aware of sounding like the philosophy elective he'd taken on a whim, where the teacher had used the word ontology for questions about what kinds of things exist, and he used it now, quietly, half-embarrassed. The current was one continuous physical fact wearing two names, or two facts we had decided to call one journey. He genuinely did not know which framing was truer, and he found he preferred not knowing to pretending.

At one o'clock the middle schoolers came through the doors like weather, jackets flapping, and Ms. Das steered them toward the wall map. Loic walked the red ribbon with his finger as he had rehearsed, warm water north along the coast, heat ferried east, palm trees in Ireland's latitude a lie but a forgivable one. A boy in a dinosaur hoodie asked why the line turned gray in the middle of the ocean, and Loic said, "It doesn't stop. Past the Grand Banks, toward Europe, it's called the North Atlantic Current," and the boy nodded as though this settled a personal grievance. The group drifted on toward the octopus tank, and their teacher lingered, a woman with a cosmopolitan accent Loic couldn't place, who said the map had confused her for years.

He stood alone with the map afterward. The red ribbon and the paler one still looked like two things to his eye, whatever his mind now insisted, and he let both readings sit side by side, unresolved. He touched the spot where the label changed, out past the Banks, where the water was the same water.

"That's where I'd put the marker," Ty said behind him, holding up a dry-erase pen he had found somewhere. "Right on the line."

"Ms. Das will kill you."

"Then let's ask her first."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York on March 25, 1911, killed 146 garment workers, many trapped because exit doors had been locked.
story:
The break room door had a union contract taped to the inside of it, and Owen read it twice while eating a granola bar he hadn't paid for yet. By happenstance his orientation had fallen on the same week the store's agreement came up for renewal, so the laminated pages were everywhere, on the time clock, in the break room, even behind the deli counter where Addyson sliced ham and narrated her opinions of management. She had opinions the way the river behind Owen's house had water, a steady riparian flow that never entirely stopped. He liked her. She had trained him on the register in forty minutes and told him that if anyone asked, the forty minutes had been four hours, because the contract said training had a minimum, and the minimum was real whether or not the training was.

The contract governed things Owen had never thought about as governable. Breaks scheduled by a formula, not by a manager's mood. Overtime paid at time and a half, which Angie explained meant "they finally pay attention to you when you cost them." A grievance procedure with numbered steps, like a recipe nobody wanted to cook. Addyson said the union got the freezer workers hazard pay two contracts ago, before Owen was even hired, and she said it with the pride of someone describing a battle she'd heard about from veterans.

It was on his third shift, pulling a pallet of canned tomatoes toward the back storage area, that he saw the fire exit. Boxes were stacked in front of it, three deep and taller than he was, and a hand truck was wedged against the push bar. He stood there long enough for the freezer's hum to become the loudest thing in the room. In his head, uninvited, Mr. Sok's eleventh-grade history class surfaced whole: the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York, March 25, 1911, one hundred forty-six garment workers dead, many of them trapped because the exit doors had been locked. Mr. Sok had made them say the number out loud. One hundred forty-six, a room of sixteen-year-olds, and Owen had thought at the time that it was a strange thing to make them do.

He tried to move the boxes and discovered they weighed more than groceries had any right to weigh, as if gravity were also management. He got two tiers down before Angie found him.

"You're going to wreck your back for eleven dollars an hour," she said.

"Isn't it eleven fifty now?"

"See, you're learning. Collective bargaining." She said it the way other people said a quarterback's name. "We voted, we bargained, they countered, we threatened a picket line with a bouncy castle, and now it's eleven fifty." The bouncy castle had apparently been Addyson's idea. It had not been needed, but the possibility of it had done work.

"The exit's blocked," Owen said. "There's a law about that, right?"

"There's a law about a lot of things. There's also a district manager who thinks the back room is a personal Tetris game." Angie looked at the boxes, then at him, and something in her face shifted from amusement to something older. "File it. Step one of the grievance thing. Paper beats heroic lifting, every time."

He filed it, which mostly meant filling out a form he had to requisition from a locked drawer because the store kept its labor documentation under the same security as its cigarettes. The union steward, a night-shift woman named nothing Owen had caught, took the form, read it, and said, "Fire exit. Good. That one they actually move on." She was right; by Friday the door was clear, a yellow line painted around it, and the district manager walked through the store radiating the specific unhappiness of a man defeated by paper.

But Owen kept turning the thing over on his lunch break, because it didn't sit flat. The store had only fixed the door because a contract and a form made it expensive not to, which meant the safety of the night crew had never been about the night crew at all. Mr. Sok would have called that structural, probably, and Owen half wanted to text him the whole story and half wanted to work it out alone. He thought about the locked doors in 1911 and the painted yellow line in the back room and understood, for the first time, that they were the same argument conducted ninety-some years apart, though he would not have claimed to know who was winning. Addyson slid into the seat across from him with her own granola bar, also unpaid for, also destined for the honor system.

"You're doing the face," she said. "The thinking face. It looks like the lifting face."

"I'm trying to figure out if anything we do here is real safety or just paperwork with good posture."

Addyson considered this while chewing. "The paperwork is what safety looks like after it's been in a fight," she said. "Now come on, register three. The bouncy castle money doesn't count itself."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A statistically significant result can still be a tiny effect: with a very large sample, even a difference too small to matter in practice can pass the significance test.
story:
Ms. Van Dijk set the folders on the desk two minutes before the bell, which everyone knew was her way of preempting the usual rush for the door. "Two articles," she said. "Same question, different answers. Your review is due Friday. It is not a book report. It is a judgment."

Ethan took his folders home and spread them on the kitchen table after dinner. The question was whether later school start times improved student grades. The first article, by a team at a large urban district, reported a statistically significant improvement after the district pushed start times back forty minutes. The second article, drawing on a different district, found no meaningful effect and argued that the first study's design had confused schedule change with a dozen other things that had changed the same year. The first article used the word significant so often that Ethan underlined it without thinking, then stopped underlining because the page went blurry with ink.

At lunch the next day he sat across from Faris, who had the same assignment. "I'm going with the first one," Faris said, tearing the crust off his sandwich. "Significant means it worked. That's the whole argument."

"It means it passed the test," Ethan said. "That's not the same as worked."

Faris looked at him the way he looked at people who corrected grammar. "Same thing."

Ethan let it go and went back to the article that evening. He found the results table on page eleven and read it four times. The improvement in the first study was there, and it was statistically significant, and the sample was enormous, tens of thousands of students across two full years. He turned back to the second article, where the author had written, almost as an aside, that with a very large sample even a difference too small to matter in practice could pass the significance test. Ethan sat with that sentence. Then he looked at the actual size of the difference in the first study, the number itself, grade point average moving by a fraction so small that no student, no parent, no teacher would ever notice it in a single report card.

He texted Edmond, who was in the other section. Did your articles have that thing where the big study found something significant but the effect was tiny. Edmond replied three minutes later: mine was about homework. the significant effect was like a quarter of a point. on a hundred point scale. Ethan read the message twice and felt something settle, not an answer exactly, but the shape of one.

In class on Thursday, Ms. Van Dijk had them draft their first paragraphs in silence. She walked the rows, stopping at Ethan's desk long enough to read over his shoulder. "You've written that the first study overstates its case," she said quietly. "Can you defend that?"

"The difference is real," Ethan said. "But it's too small to matter. The sample was huge, and with a very large sample even a tiny difference passes the significance test. So when they call it significant, they're right about the test and wrong about what people will hear."

Faris, two rows over, turned around. "So which one wins?"

"That's the wrong question," Ethan said, and heard how it sounded, like something off a poster, so he pushed on before anyone could laugh. "The second article's district didn't do a better study. It just did a different one. I think the honest answer is that later start times probably help, but not enough that you'd notice, and nobody's measured it in a way that settles it. That's my review."

Ms. Van Dijk offered the class a deal before the bell: anyone who wanted could turn in a rough draft that afternoon for comments, with the promise that anything wrong in the draft would carry no penalty, a kind of amnesty for bad first attempts. Half the room stayed. Faris did not. He shoved his folder into his bag and said, "I'm not rewriting mine," in a truculent voice that made the girl next to him glance up.

Ethan stayed. He printed his draft, walked it to the front desk, and set it down on the stack. Ms. Van Dijk picked it up and read the last line while he stood there, the line that said the evidence was thin in both directions and that the first study's significant result was, in practice, almost nothing. She looked at him over the page.

"That's a hard sentence to write," she said. "Most students pick a side."

"I tried," Ethan said. "It wouldn't stick."

She wrote something in the margin and handed the draft back. He carried it to his desk, folded it once, and put it in his bag next to the two articles, still side by side, still disagreeing.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: Denmark, Norway and Sweden have no statutory national minimum wage; pay floors are instead set through collective agreements between unions and employers.
story:
The break room at Ferraro's Market smelled of wet cardboard and the lemon solvent Hayden mopped the aisles with, and the schedule taped inside the door said his Saturday shift had been quietly extended from five hours to seven. He stared at the handwriting, his father's voice in his head, from the dinner table two years ago, when the plant had voted on whether to organize: "You don't bite the hand that feeds you, but you don't let it slap you either." Hayden had been fourteen then, half-listening, and had metabolized the sentence only later, after he'd started working for Mr. Ferraro himself.

Walter, who worked the register and had failed senior math twice, leaned against the sink eating a granola bar with his back teeth. "Fourteen an hour," Walter said, crumbs on his chin. "That's what they pay the union guys at the warehouse my cousin works at. Bag boys and cashiers here, we're at eleven."

"There's a debate on Thursday," Hayden said. "School thing. Minimum wage. Oliver's on the other side and he's been reading for weeks."

"Debate," Walter repeated, as though the word belonged to a different country.

The subject had seemed simple when Mr. Mansour, the economics teacher who ran the debate club, handed out the motion: the minimum wage should be raised. Hayden had taken the affirmative without thinking. Then, on Tuesday night, hunting through library databases at the long table under the buzzing light, he found a table of countries and stopped with his finger on the page. Denmark, Norway, Sweden. No statutory national minimum wage at all. He read the sentence three times. Those were the countries everyone held up as decent places, high wages, and they had no legal minimum written anywhere. Instead the pay floors came through collective agreements, unions and employers bargaining them into contracts, sector by sector. He copied it onto his index card and sat for a while not moving, because the card fit neither side of the motion.

"Read it again," Oliver said at lunch on Wednesday, chewing a sandwich, his notebook open to a page of numbered arguments.

"Denmark, Norway and Sweden have no statutory national minimum wage. Pay floors are set through collective agreements between unions and employers."

Oliver's mouth stopped mid-bite. "Then how does anyone get paid?"

"That's the point. That's what I can't figure out."

"You're supposed to be arguing for a raise."

"I know what I'm supposed to do."

On Thursday the debate club met in the stuffy portable classroom, and Oliver went first, smooth and loud, citing employment effects, calling a high wage floor a disincentive to hiring. When Hayden stood, his prepared speech was in his hand and he didn't use it. "The countries with no legal minimum at all have strong unions," he said. "Denmark, Norway, Sweden, no statutory national minimum wage, and wages get set by collective bargaining, unions and employers, agreements instead of laws. So the fight isn't only about the number. It's about who's in the room when the number gets decided."

"That helps me," Oliver said, delighted, which was not the response Hayden had planned for.

Afterward Mr. Mansour collected the notecards without comment, and Hayden walked to work through the cold with his collar up, turning the portable classroom's argument over the way he turned a stuck wheel on a shopping cart, testing where it gave. At Ferraro's, Walter was at the register and the store was empty except for a woman comparing two kinds of vinegar. In the break room, two of the stockers, both older than Hayden's mother, were talking in low voices, and one of them slid a photocopied sheet across the table as Hayden clocked in. A petition. It asked for fixed schedules, a written schedule posted a week ahead, and a raise to thirteen dollars. At the bottom it said something about contacting a union representative.

"Are you in?" the stocker asked. Her name tag said Rosa, but everyone called her the flower lady because she trimmed the bouquets nobody bought.

"I'm sixteen," Hayden said.

"Sixteen-year-olds get scheduled too."

He signed it, and his signature looked small on the line. Then he thought of Mr. Ferraro, who had once driven Hayden home in the rain when his bike chain snapped, and who also rewrote the schedule in pen whenever a delivery truck ran late, and both of those facts sat in him side by side without one cancelling the other. Maybe the union was right and maybe it would cost shifts; the Nordic thing proved only that there were doors he hadn't known existed, not which one to walk through. He could hold that. He was getting practice at holding things.

Saturday, Mr. Ferraro came around the registers at closing with the cash bag under his arm. He paused at the schedule taped to the break room door, where Rosa's pen had added a question mark next to the new hours. He stood there for a long moment, the tectonic silence of a man deciding what kind of manager he was, and then he took the schedule down, folded it, and put it in his shirt pocket without a word.

"What do we work off tomorrow?" Hayden asked him.

"Put up the old one," Mr. Ferraro said. "The five-hour one."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Pride and Prejudice, the Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr Collins, so none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home.
story:
Tristan had claimed the reading nook by the window with a thermos, two notebooks, and his mother's copy of Pride and Prejudice, which smelled faintly of the spice drawer it had lived in since 2009. On the laptop propped against the cushion, Alisha's face pixelated, then resolved. Behind her, Daniela waved with a pen in her hand.

"He wants a thesis," Tristan said. "Ms. Kaya. One paragraph tonight, or we're not allowed to run the session."

"Which she's paying you an honorarium for," Daniela said. "Ten whole dollars from the programming budget. Don't spend it all at once."

"It's the principle of the thing. It means I'm a professional now." He straightened the notebook as though professionalism were a posture. The library ran the book club on Thursdays, and this Thursday, for reasons Tristan had not fully examined before volunteering, he was the discussion leader.

Alisha held up her copy, a rubber band around it. "Okay, so I reread the chapters Mrs Bennet is in, and I take back everything I said last week. Everybody treats her like she's ridiculous, obsessed with marrying off the girls, embarrassing at the assembly. But look." She flipped to a dog-eared page. "The estate is entailed to Mr Collins. A male heir, some cousin they've never met. Five daughters, and none of them can inherit their father's home."

"So when Mr Bennet dies, they're out," Daniela said slowly.

"They're out. The house, the land, all of it goes to this garrulous little clergyman who writes letters that take a full page to say nothing." Alisha let that sit. "So the matchmaking, the nerves, the whole performance. It's not hysteria. It's math."

Tristan wrote match making = math and then crossed it out, because it looked stupid. "That's the feminist reading," he said. "Or part of it. She's read as a joke because she's responding rationally to a system that's irrational."

"It's also the Marxist reading," Daniela said, and Tristan's pen stopped. "Marriage as the only transfer of property available to them. The girls don't have careers, they don't have inheritance, so the marriage market is the market. Charlotte marries Mr Collins for the house and everyone acts like she's the tragic one, but she's the only person negotiating honestly."

"That's grim."

"She says she asks only a comfortable home. Which is what the entail already took off the table."

Tristan sat back against the window frame. Outside, a neighbor dragged a recycling bin up the driveway with the concentration of a man defusing something. He had assumed the assignment meant picking a lens, the way you picked a club. Feminist or Marxist, choose one, argue it cleanly, collect the honorarium. But Alisha and Daniela were both right, and their arguments weren't competing so much as overlapping, two windows into the same cold room, and he said so.

"Both lenses land on the same fact," he said, writing as he talked now. "The entail is the engine. Take it away and Mrs Bennet is a fool and Charlotte is a sellout. Keep it and they're both making the best trades in a rigged market. Even Wickham, who absconds to London with Lydia and nearly ruins the family, is doing the same thing the rest of them do with better manners. He's converting charm into money because that's the only conversion available."

Alisha pointed at him through the screen. "Put that in the paragraph."

"Which part?"

"The rigged market. But you have to be honest about what you can't prove," she said. "We're reading the system through the women. We don't actually know what the entail law says beyond what the novel needs it to do. Austen doesn't explain it. She just lets it press on everybody."

"That's true," Tristan admitted. "We're inferring the cage from how the bird flies." He wrote that down too, then considered whether it was too much, and decided the professional thing was to let the professionals decide. He read his draft aloud, the part about Mrs Bennet's nerves being an economic instrument, the part where he admitted the lenses agreed more than they disagreed and that the disagreement, mostly about whether Charlotte was to be pitied, was where Thursday's fight would happen.

"Good," Daniela said. "Start there, with Charlotte. I'll bring the counterargument."

"You're going to defend her or attack her?"

"I'll decide when I see the room," Daniela said, and uncapped her pen.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
Hannah had forty minutes before her mother's lunch meeting ended, and the office was quiet enough that she could hear the vending machine humming down the hall. She had come in to print her registration forms because the home printer had died mid-page, and while the sheets fed through, she had opened the video her group chat was already fighting about. The clip showed a flooded street, a man wading past a floating car, and text claiming it was their city, that morning. Mark had shared it with the message "we need to do something about this NOW." Eleven people had already forwarded it.

The printer jammed on page three. Hannah pulled the paper tray out, and a woman from the neighboring cubicle leaned over the divider. Ms. Shevchenko, the compliance officer, who had once told Hannah that her job was mostly making people slow down before they signed things. "You look like you're about to forward something," Ms. Shevchenko said. "That's the exact face I'm paid to prevent."

"It's a flood video," Hannah said. "Mark says it's from this morning, by the river."

"Is it?" Ms. Shevchenko straightened a stack of files on her desk, the whole surface ruled with manila chronology, dated tabs in strict order. "Because I've lived here nineteen years, and I remember a flood that looked a lot like that."

Hannah stopped scrolling. That was the whole problem, she realized. She didn't know if it was from this morning, and the fight in the group chat was already a hundred messages deep, everyone arguing about whose fault the drainage was. Amelie had written, "If it's real we should organize a drive by Friday." A drive, with real boxes, based on a clip nobody had checked. The deadline was suddenly not abstract. Amelie wanted an answer before sixth period tomorrow.

She remembered a workshop from spring semester, a guest speaker who had walked them through something called SIFT. She couldn't recall the speaker's name, only the letters, and she typed them into the search bar to emancipate herself from her own memory instead of guessing. Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to their original context. She read it twice. Then she did what the letters told her to do, in order, because the order was the point.

First she stopped. She put the phone face down on the printer tray and finished freeing page three, which felt ridiculous and also helped. Then she investigated the source: the account that posted it had no name, no location, and nine videos, all disasters. Then she found better coverage. She searched "flood floating car" with the name of her city and got nothing from any local outlet, not one, which for an event that big was its own kind of answer. Ms. Shevchenko, still watching, said, "Nineteen years. I'd bet my lanyard it was oh-eight." The office air conditioning clicked on. Then Hannah traced the claim to its original context, which turned out to be the part she'd never known was possible: she took a screenshot of a frame from the video and ran it through a reverse image search. The results came back immediately. The same footage, uploaded six years ago, in a province of a different country, captioned in a language Hannah couldn't read. The man wading past the car was wading past it in 2019.

She sat back. The vending machine hummed. "It's not even our river," she said.

"Congratulations," Ms. Shevchenko said. "You've just done more verification than most of this building does before replying all."

Hannah picked up the phone and typed to Mark: "Don't share that. Reverse image search it. It's from six years ago, different country." Then, because she wasn't sure how much one check proved, she added, "I could be wrong about the details, but the date isn't." That was the honest version. She knew what she'd found, and she also knew she'd checked exactly one thing, once, on office wifi, with twenty-two minutes left before her mother came back. The clip was old. Whether the river could still flood like that, whether the drainage argument had merit, whether Amelie's drive was a bad idea or only a badly sourced one, those stayed open, and Hannah left them open on purpose, the way Ms. Shevchenko left a file's later tabs blank until the facts arrived.

Amelie replied fast: "Wait, you can search an image backward? Teach me at lunch." Then Mark: "Deleting it. My aunt sent it to me first, so blame her." Hannah printed the last page, straightened the stack of forms, and wrote her name at the top.

Ms. Shevchenko dropped a highlighter over the divider. "For the tabs," she said. "You'll want a system."

"I have a system," Hannah said, holding up her phone. "It has four letters and it starts with S."

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, set up in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme, does no original research; it assesses the published scientific literature.
story:
Oliver had reserved the study room at the public library for four o'clock, and by four ten the table was already buried. Antony spread out his debate binder, tapped a highlighted paragraph, and said, "Here's our strongest point. The IPCC runs all these climate experiments, so nobody can argue the findings are fringe."

Oliver pulled the binder toward him across the table. Outside the study room's glass wall, an old man was shelving returns, moving with the slow deliberateness of someone who had done it for years. A boy at the computers clicked a mouse in bursts. "Runs experiments," Oliver repeated. He didn't like the loose feeling of the sentence, though he couldn't yet say why.

"That's the whole point of them existing," Antony said. "They're the science side."

Enzo arrived at four fifteen with two coffees and his usual posture of cheerful combat. He slid into the third chair and said, "Before we go further, I want it on record that I'm the dissident here. I think the resolution is rigged. But go on, tell me about the experiments."

"You're not a dissident, you're just contrary," Antony said, but he was grinning.

Oliver was only half listening. The name had snagged on something. He could picture Mr. Martínez's classroom from the spring, the afternoon light coming in flat and dusty, the way their teacher had stood beside the projector with his arms folded and refused to tell them things. When a student had asked him whether the IPCC was trustworthy, Mr. Martínez had said, "Look it up and tell me tomorrow," and the next day, when the student came back with a half answer, Mr. Martínez had only nodded and asked a harder question. Oliver had resented it then. It felt like being handed a map with the streets left off. Now, in the study room, he wondered whether that had been the whole lesson, that the streets had to be walked by the person holding the map.

He turned to the library computer and typed the name into the catalogue, then, finding nothing there, into the search bar on the browser. The screensaver on the monitor next to his flickered through photographs of glaciers. He read, scrolled, read again. "Antony. Sit down for a second."

"I am sitting."

"The IPCC doesn't run experiments." Oliver kept his voice low because of the glass wall, though nobody out there was listening. "It's not a lab. It was set up in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme, and it does no original research at all. It assesses the published scientific literature. That's what it does. It reads what everyone else has already published and weighs it."

Antony leaned over Oliver's shoulder, and the backlight caught the confusion moving across his face. "Then what was I citing?"

"A name you thought meant something else." Enzo had gone uncharacteristically quiet, chin on his fist, watching them both. "So the experiments," he said slowly, "happen somewhere else. Universities. Government labs. Whoever."

"Whoever publishes," Oliver said. He scrolled further, past the screen's edge of blue, and found the part about how the assessment worked, thousands of studies drawn together, findings checked against each other. Nobody in the room said anything for a moment. Down the aisle the shelver dropped a book, and the small flat sound of it seemed to organize the silence.

"So my strongest point," Antony said, "is built on me not knowing what the organization actually is."

"That's one way to put it," Enzo said, with what he probably imagined was kindness.

"Here's the thing, though." Oliver pulled the binder back and flipped to the highlighted paragraph, then to the blank page after it. "It might be a stronger point now. If it were one lab, one set of experiments, you could vilify the people running them and the whole thing wobbles. But this is an organization that just reads. It's assessing what's already been published, over and over, by people who didn't coordinate with each other. The strength isn't in any single result. It's in the repetition." He was working this out as he spoke, and he could hear the seams in it, places where he was guessing. "I think. I'd want to check how the assessment actually gets done before we put it in the case."

Antony's effusive relief had started to show, shoulders dropping, pen already moving, but Enzo held up a hand. "You're sure the repetition means what you think it means? Studies get things wrong all the time. They get published wrong."

"I'm not sure," Oliver said. He wrote three lines on the blank page, crossed one out, and wrote a fourth. "That's what the next hour is for." He pointed his pen at the stacks behind the glass, where the science section began at the low shelf under the window, and stood up.

"You're going to make me read the actual reports," Antony said.

"We're going to read them," Oliver said, and pushed open the study room door.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Montana is the one US state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.
story:
Charlotte filled out the application at the kitchen table while her mother washed dishes, the form curling under her palm because the pen was dying and she had to press hard. The Greenhouse Garden Center was hiring for the spring, ten hours a week, mostly watering and hauling bags of soil out to customers' cars. Mr. Villanueva owned it. He had been her neighbor since she was six, the man who gave out full-sized candy bars on Halloween and once dug her mother's car out of a snowbank without being asked.

"He'll hire you," her mother said, not turning from the sink. "That's the problem, actually."

Charlotte didn't ask what she meant. She knew. If Mr. Villanueva hired her because he knew her, then she would never be sure she'd been hired for any other reason, and every mistake she made at the garden center would feel like it was being weighed against twelve years of borrowed ladders and Christmas cards. She signed her name and folded the form into her backpack anyway, because she wanted the job more than she wanted the certainty.

That night she video-called her cousin Ryan, who lived in Billings and had been working at a grocery store since October. Ryan was seventeen and liked to talk like the world was arranged in a series of rigged games. When she told him about the job, he laughed.

"You know your boss can fire you just because he's in a bad mood, right? Like you burn his toast one morning and you're gone."

"That's not how it works."

"That's exactly how it works. I looked it up. Except here, weirdly. Montana is the one state where it's different. After a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker. It's called the Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act. 1987. Everywhere else, bad mood, you're out."

"It's called what?"

"The Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act," Ryan said again, slower, the way he said things when he thought you weren't listening. "Look it up if you don't believe me."

She did look it up, after they hung up, sitting on her bed with her laptop warming her thighs. He had it right. She read it twice, then sat for a while looking at the curtain, which had come unhooked at one corner and hung crooked, its pattern of small blue leaves interrupted at the fold. There was something strange about the fact. It didn't change anything for her, since she didn't live in Montana, and yet it changed how she thought about the whole arrangement. The rules she'd assumed were fixed, like weather, were actually a choice someone had made, in one place, in 1987, and made differently everywhere else.

The interview was on a Thursday afternoon. Mr. Villanueva sat on an overturned pot in the back of the greenhouse, between racks of seedlings that smelled like wet earth, and asked her the questions he was probably supposed to ask. Then he asked her one he wasn't.

"Why do you want this job?"

She had prepared an answer about learning responsibility and liking plants. Instead she heard herself say, "I want to know if I can be good at something where nobody has to be nice to me."

He looked at her for a long moment, the way he looked at seed packets, she thought, reading something on the surface that stood for something underneath. She wondered if the question had impugned him, if he heard it as an accusation that his kindness wasn't real. She hadn't meant that. Or she had meant it a little, and she was sorry and not sorry at the same time, because both things were true: he was kind, and his kindness made it harder for her to know things about herself.

"Start Saturday," he said. "Eight in the morning. And Charlotte, if you're late, I'm not going to fire you. I'm going to be annoyed, and I'll tell you so, and you'll come in earlier the next time."

The following week Derek, who was in her English class and had gotten himself fired from a sandwich shop in February, sat on her front steps while she repotted a basil plant she'd bought with her first paycheck. Derek's position was that bosses were a phenomenonology of moods, by which he seemed to mean that you never dealt with the boss himself, only with whatever weather he was having that day, and Derek's own firing had coincided with a thunderstorm of one. Charlotte told him about Montana, about the act with its long careful name, and about the probationary period, and Derek said, "So there's one place where the weather doesn't decide," and she said, "Generally, after a while, no."

She was still turning it over. She couldn't decide whether Ryan's Montana was a better world or just a safer one, whether good cause was a floor to stand on or a wall that kept you in rooms you'd chosen too quickly. She only knew she wanted to find out from the inside, with dirt under her nails and a boss who told her the truth when she was late.

She pressed the soil down around the basil with her thumb, firm but not hard, the way Mr. Villanueva had shown her, and watered it until the surplus ran clear from the bottom of the pot.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
story:
The cart wobbled on its bad left wheel as Riley steered it past the dairy case, and he kept one eye on the list his mother had texted him and the other on his phone's clock. He had an hour and a half before his mother got home from her double shift, and the plan was a whole dinner, roasted chicken and rice and the green beans she liked, done and on the table so she didn't have to stand up again after twelve hours on her feet. He had saved the money from mowing lawns all August. He had watched the same video three times, pausing to write down temperatures.

The trouble started in the parking lot. He had just loaded the bags into the trunk when his phone rang, and it was Maxym, whose car had died two blocks from the store and whose voice had that flat, careful sound it got when he was trying not to ask for help. Riley said yes before he thought about the groceries, and then stood a second with his hand still on the trunk, doing arithmetic he didn't like. It was ninety-four degrees out, the kind of heat that made the asphalt go soft and shimmering. He had a cooler in the garage at home and nothing here but canvas bags and a bottle of water.

He left the bags where they were and jogged the two blocks. Maxym's car needed a jump, and the woman at the house with the jumper cables had a dog that had to be coaxed inside first, and the whole thing took longer than it should have because Maxym kept apologizing and Riley kept saying it was fine, which made everything slower. When the engine finally caught, Maxym drove him back to the lot. Riley had been gone a little over an hour.

Ms. Kelly from next door was pushing her own cart toward the entrance as he popped the trunk, and she stopped when she saw him standing there not moving, staring at the bags. "You look like a man at a funeral," she said.

"Sort of," Riley said. "The chicken's been in there since before I left." He lifted the bag and it was warm on the bottom, warm like a hand. The milk beside it, the package of cut-up meat for tomorrow. He had read something once, half-remembered, about how long food could sit out, but he couldn't make it resolve into numbers he trusted.

"Call somebody who knows," Ms. Kelly said. "Don't guess at it. That's how people get sick, guessing."

He called Cecilia, who was spending her summer reading everything the internet had to offer and arguing about it, and who answered on the second ring. "Okay," she said when he explained, "this is actually one of the things I know. Food safety guidance. Perishable food shouldn't sit between forty and a hundred forty degrees for more than two hours. And if it's over ninety out, which it is, then it's one hour, not two." She said it fast, the way she recited things, and then slower, because she could hear him breathing. "How long, Riley?"

"An hour," he said. "Maybe a little more. I don't know exactly when I put them in."

"That's not a thing you don't know exactly," Cecilia said. "That's the whole thing. You have to know."

He sat on the bumper of Maxym's car with the phone against his ear and looked at the carton of milk, the chicken in its padded package, the rice and the canned beans and the onions sitting untouched in a separate bag. Maxym leaned against the car and waited without saying anything, which was its own kind of kindness. Riley understood that there were two ways to think about it. One was the way his grandmother would have gone, the waste-not way, where you cooked the chicken thoroughly and trusted the oven. The other was the way Cecilia had just handed him, where the numbers were the numbers and an hour in a hot trunk in ninety-four-degree heat had already used up whatever margin he had. His mother would say throw it out, food is cheaper than a hospital bill. His grandmother would have exhumed last week's leftovers from the back of the fridge and served them without fear. Both of them were sure, and he envied the certainty more than he could say.

"I don't know exactly when I put the bags in," he said finally, "so I have to count it as more than an hour. That's the honest way to do it." He wasn't sure the chicken would actually hurt anyone. That was the part that stayed uncertain, the part nobody could promise him either direction. But if he didn't know the time, he couldn't claim the time, and he found he didn't want to claim it. "The chicken and the milk go," he told Cecilia. "I'll get more."

"That's the right call," she said, and then, because she was Cecilia, "Also your onions are fine. Onions are basically rocks."

He carried the warm bags to the store's trash can by the door, and it felt like a kind of attrition, this steady losing of things he'd paid for, money going out of the world a bag at a time. Inside, he went back through the cool of the dairy aisle and the meat case with his remaining cash, doing the subtraction as he walked. He bought a smaller chicken and a quart of milk instead of a gallon. The green beans were gone, so he got frozen ones, and in the checkout line he picked up a dented package of cookies that had been marked down, the shortbread gone slightly friable at one corner where the box had taken the hit. He put it on the belt anyway. His mother liked shortbread, and the package was sealed.

Ms. Kelly was two registers over, and she caught his eye and raised her chin at him, once, like a salute. He raised his back. At home the new chicken went straight into the oven, and he set the timer, and while it roasted he called his mother at work and told her the whole thing, the dead battery, the hot trunk, the hour he couldn't account for. She was quiet for a moment on the line.

"You did the right thing," she said. "Now tell Maxym he owes you a chicken."

"He already knows," Riley said, and slid the pan a quarter turn, watching the skin begin to brown.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
story:
The afternoon lane swimmers had thinned to two by the time Ashley climbed the tall chair at the deep end, whistle looped around her wrist because the lanyard pinched her neck. It was her fourth shift as a lifeguard and her first week of paid work of any kind, and she was still learning to sit that high above people without feeling like she was eavesdropping on the world. Devon was on the shallow end, feet swinging, and between them the water held the late light in long plates of orange. She liked this part of the day. She had not liked the part before it.

At her break, the memory sat with her at the picnic table behind the pump house, where she ate a sandwich she couldn't finish.
