They ran scene one and it went well enough that Faith let herself relax, and then scene two began and fell apart inside thirty seconds. Lucian crossed left while Caitlin crossed right, they met in the middle near the paper lamp that stood for the kitchen table, and Caitlin sidestepped, and Lucian sidestepped the same way, and they laughed, and then they weren't laughing, they were just stuck, two people bumping and apologizing in a small warm pool of stage light.

"Okay," Faith said, when they'd tried it four more times and it had gone wrong four different ways. She sat down on the stage edge and made herself cogitate instead of panic, because panicking was easy and thinking was the only thing she was actually good at. Somewhere in her mother's stack of theatre books, the ones with cracked spines she'd been reading all month, there had been a word for exactly this. She couldn't find the word, only the shape of it, the idea that movement on a stage was a thing a director planned instead of a thing that happened.

Ms. Asante, who taught chemistry three doors down but had acted all through her twenties, came in on Tuesday to pick up the garrulous old boom mic the theatre had borrowed from the science wing. She stayed to watch one run of scene two and winced, audibly, at the second collision. Faith expected a speech, a correction, some adult certainty handed over like a marked exam. Instead Ms. Asante asked, "Have you blocked it?"

"Blocked it?"

"It's called blocking," Ms. Asante said. "The planned positioning and movement of actors on stage. The director sets it during rehearsals." Then she looked at her watch, said she had a lab at eleven, and left Faith holding the word like something warm.

So it had a name, and the name was not the answer, and that was somehow the most useful thing Faith learned all week. Her arrows were already blocking; they were just bad blocking, dreamed up at her desk instead of built out of real bodies in a real room. On Thursday she did it differently. She put Lucian and Caitlin where scene two started, walked the stage herself, said their lines under her breath, and felt where the pull was, where the moment wanted him to move. She set the cross to the window on Caitlin's line, then found the flaw she'd never seen on paper: her own tape mark for the lamp sat directly in the path, an encumbrance she had drawn and then forgotten. She pulled the lamp a foot upstage, re-taped, wrote it down.

"Again," she said, "from the top of the scene," and this time she didn't watch the script, she watched the floor. Lucian crossed on the line, Caitlin let him pass, and the moment that had collapsed all week held, and held, and landed. It still wasn't right, exactly; the pause before Caitlin's reply went on too long, and Faith didn't know yet whether that was a mistake or a discovery. She stood in the dark past the tape marks with her pencil hovering over the page, unwilling to fix what she hadn't decided was broken.

"One more time," Caitlin called from the window, already back in place. "Before my mom comes."

Faith lifted her hand. "Scene two, from the top."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: In NLRB v. J. Weingarten (1975), the US Supreme Court ruled that unionized workers may request a union representative at an interview they reasonably believe could lead to discipline.
story:
Laurence clocked in at six, the same minute the automatic doors began their evening stutter, and found the break room corkboard stripped bare. The new schedule was supposed to be up by Friday. It was Saturday, and Sunday's closing shift, the one she had traded away three weeks ago to study for finals, had her name back on it in Ms. Ito's tidy ballpoint. She stood in front of the board with her apron half over her head, doing the arithmetic she hated: the exam Monday morning, the store's rule that no one leaves before the floor is recovered, and no manager anywhere on the floor to ask.

Rory was already collecting carts in the lot, collars up against the wind, and through the glass he looked like a boy being slowly erased. He wanted the extra hours, that was the thing; his brother had moved out and the rent split had moved with him. When Laurence waved him inside, he came reluctantly, releasing a cart that rolled off on its own. "If you give up the Sunday close," he said, "I'll take it. I already asked Ms. Ito. She said the swap has to come from you, not from her, because of the seniority rules. Something about the contract." He said the word carefully, as if it were breakable. Laurence had worked here fourteen months and never once thought about the contract; she had ascribed her paycheck, her breaks, even the rubber mat behind the register, to the general kindness of the store, which she now suspected was not the store's motivation at all.

Ms. Ito appeared at the end of aisle six with a clipboard and the expression of someone whose evening had already gone wrong before it started. "There's a spill on nine," she said, "and then I need you in the office for a minute. Someone says the till was short Thursday, on your drawer." Laurence's face went hot before her mind caught up. Thursday she remembered perfectly: the coupon arbitrage some customers ran, stacking a manufacturer's discount on a store discount until the register owed them money, and Mr. Pell at the service desk waving every discrepancy through because it was easier than arguing. But the short till had her number on it, and the office had Mr. Pell's cousin in it, the one who did the auditing.

"I didn't take anything," she said. "I know," Ms. Ito said, not unkindly, and turned toward the office, and it was in the turning that Laurence noticed Simran from the deli counter watching, wiping her hands on her apron with deliberate slowness. Simran was older, twenty-two maybe, and had a lanyard with a yellow card on it that Laurence had seen a thousand times without reading. "Wait," Simran said, just loudly enough. "You're union. You know you can have somebody in there with you." Laurence looked at her. "In the office?" "If it's the kind of interview you think might end in discipline. That's the rule. It came down in a Supreme Court case, NLRB versus J. Weingarten, 1975. Unionized workers can ask for a rep." Simran said it flat and fast, a line worn smooth from saying it to every new hire the union never quite got to.

Laurence stood in the corridor between the dairy case and the office door and felt the two thoughts grind against each other. One was simple fear: take Simran in there and Mr. Pell's cousin would mark her as trouble, and trouble didn't get the good shifts, and Rory was standing right there wanting exactly the shift she was about to jeopardize. The other thought was slower and colder: the schedule being late, the swap rule, the spill that conveniently emptied the floor, the fact that no one had ever told her she could have someone beside her, and that the not-telling was probably not an accident. She could ascribe her hesitation to prudence, but she suspected it was closer to cowardice wearing prudence's coat, and there was no time to sort out which, because Ms. Ito was holding the door.

"Simran," she said. "Will you come in with me?" The request felt strange in her mouth, formal, like borrowing a phrase from a language she was only beginning to speak. Simran pulled off her apron and hung it on the hook by the time clock, unhurried, making the small ceremony visible. "Yes," she said. "That's what the yellow card is for."

The office was small and smelled of toner. Mr. Pell's cousin had a printout arranged with prolix thoroughness, every void, every override, Thursday's discrepancies marching down two pages, and at the top, circled, the number from her drawer. But before he began, Laurence said, "Before we start, is this something that could end in discipline?" and when he glanced at Ms. Ito and did not say no, Simran set the yellow card on the desk, and the cousin's whole manner reorganized itself, the way a room does when a window is opened.

They were in there forty minutes. The Sunday shift came up exactly once, near the end, when the cousin, retreat completed, offered to smooth the schedule as a gesture of goodwill, and Laurence looked at the closed door and thought of Rory out in the lot with the carts. She said she'd think about it. When she finally came out, it was past nine, and through the front glass she could see him still collecting, one cart at a time, while the register lights hummed down the dark aisles. Simran put her apron back on at the time clock. "You'll give him the shift," she said, not as a question. Laurence pushed through the swinging door into the cold of the produce section and started toward the lot, still wearing her name tag, to find out.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by communication researcher Jeffrey Hall estimated it takes roughly 50 hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
The new house smelled like paint and cold dust, and Emilie sat on the floor of her empty bedroom with her phone against her knee, counting. Three weeks. Fifteen school days. She had been keeping a list in her notes app, times and places, like a scientist who didn't trust herself to remember honestly. Matteo: 11 hours, mostly in physics, mostly talking about the problem sets. Blaine: 6 hours, half of that a bus ride to a meet where they'd barely spoken. Nobody else made the list at all.

She'd found the number at two in the morning, unable to sleep on the inflatable mattress, scrolling through her feed in the dark. A communication researcher named Jeffrey Hall had done a study in 2018, and the estimate that came out of it was that it takes roughly fifty hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. Fifty. She had done the arithmetic so many times the digits felt worn smooth. At eleven hours, Matteo wasn't even a quarter of the way to casual.

The floorboards in the hallway shifted, and her mother appeared in the doorway with two mugs. "The kitchen's not hooked up, so it's instant." She lowered herself against the wall, and they drank in the room where Emilie's bed was supposed to go. "Your grandmother wants to know when you'll come recuperate at her place for a weekend. She thinks the country air will fix whatever's wrong with you."

"Nothing's wrong with me." Emilie set the mug down. "There's a study. This guy Hall, in 2018, he figured out it takes about fifty hours together before an acquaintance becomes a casual friend. I've done maybe eleven hours with the closest person at that school. So when Grandma asks why I haven't made friends yet, that's why. It's arithmetic, not a character flaw."

Her mother was quiet for a second. "You're keeping score?"

"I'm keeping data." It came out sharper than she meant, and she softened it by handing the mug back. "It's not sad. It's just where I am on the curve."

The next afternoon Mr. Leblanc kept her after history. He'd assigned a historiography project, two students per topic, and he'd paired her with Matteo, which was how she'd gotten most of her eleven hours in the first place. "You write like someone who thinks evidence settles things," he said, tapping her draft. "It doesn't. It argues. That's the whole discipline."

She took the paper back and didn't answer, because answering would have meant telling him about the list, and about how Blaine had cornered her at lunch and demanded to see it. That had been yesterday. Blaine, who talked so prolix through fourth period that even the substitute had stopped trying to steer him, had read the numbers off her screen and then gone very quiet, which was worse than anything he could have said.

"Eleven hours," he'd said finally. "That's what I am to you. A data point."

"That's not what it means."

"Then what does it mean?"

She hadn't had an answer, and the silence had lasted until the bell. Now, walking home through streets she still had to navigate by map, she turned the whole thing over. Her grandmother's cure, her mother's skepticism, Mr. Leblanc's insistence that evidence argued rather than settled, and Blaine's face at lunch, hurt in a way the number hadn't predicted. Maybe the study measured time because time was measurable, and not because time was the thing itself. Maybe what happened inside the hours mattered in a way hours couldn't record, and maybe it didn't, and she couldn't tell yet. She held both ideas the way you hold two stones, one in each hand, unable to weigh them against each other.

The new house stood at the end of the street with its FOR SALE sign finally gone from the lawn. Inside, the rooms echoed, and her footsteps on the bare boards sounded like someone else's. She sat down in the empty living room, opened her phone, and deleted the list. Then, before she could think better of it, she typed a message to Blaine: want to work on the Hall thing? I'll explain. No, that wasn't right either. She deleted that too. In a new school three weeks in, she texted the only sentence she actually meant: "free tonight? I have instant coffee and no furniture." She set the phone face up on the floor beside her and listened to it buzz once, sharp in the hollow room.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Some leases require the tenant to carry renter's insurance, which covers the tenant's own belongings rather than the building and adds a monthly premium.
story:
The driving school on Route 9 smelled like burnt coffee and vinyl, and Mr. Vu had already confiscated Evan's phone twice before the ten-minute break. Ryan spread two apartment leases across the fold-out desk, a calculator balanced on his knee, and highlighted a line in the Hazel Street lease for the third time as if the ink might change its mind.

"You're doing homework," Lilly said, dropping into the seat beside him with her slushie. "At driving school. That's like doing taxes at a water park."

"Mom wants an answer by Friday," Ryan said. "Hazel Street or Pinecrest. Both near campus, both one bedroom, both boring." He tapped the pages. "Hazel Street is nine hundred a month, utilities included. Pinecrest is eight twenty plus utilities, and the utilities average about ninety, according to the girl showing it. So Pinecrest is cheaper by roughly ten dollars, except I can't make the numbers come out, because my mom's budget worksheet says I should have sixty left over each month and I keep getting forty."

"Forty is forty," Evan said, leaning over from the row behind. "Some people have zero. Some people have negative zero, which is a thing I've reified personally."

"That's not what that word means," Lilly said.

"It means I made it real. My bank account made my broke-ness real." Evan stole a sip of her slushie and dodged the swat. "Anyway, look at the fine print, man. Fine print is where leases hide their crimes."

Ryan read the fine print. He read it again. Then he sat back in the plastic chair, which squeaked like a dying accordion, and said, "Oh, you have got to be kidding."

"What?"

"Pinecrest requires renter's insurance." He turned the lease so they could see it, the clause small and confident at the bottom of page four. "It's a policy the tenant has to carry, and it covers your own stuff, your belongings, not the building. And it's a monthly premium on top of everything."

"So add it in," Lilly said, with the calm of someone whose problems were currently limited to parallel parking.

"That's the thing. I called the insurance place during the vending machine run. Twelve dollars a month." Ryan punched the calculator with a vengeance. "So Pinecrest is eight twenty plus ninety utilities plus twelve insurance, that's nine twenty-two. Hazel Street is nine hundred flat, no insurance requirement, no utilities. The whole comparison flips. The cheap apartment was never the cheap apartment."

Mr. Vu drifted over during the break, hands clasped behind his back like an irascible penguin inspecting the ice. He looked at the leases, the highlighters, the calculator, and said only, "This is a driving school, Mr. Ryan."

"I'm learning to compare," Ryan said. "It's basically the same skill."

"It is not the same skill."

"It's assessing risk versus cost. You told us that on Tuesday. You said, and I quote, 'Driving is risk management with a steering wheel.'"

Mr. Vu's mouth did something that was almost a smile before he suppressed it on principle. "Tuesday's lesson contains no such aphorism."

"It does. Evan heard it."

"I heard something," Evan agreed, unhelpfully. "There may have been a steering wheel."

The break ended. Mr. Vu resumed the lesson on three-point turns, and Ryan's highlighter went back in his bag, but his mind stayed on the two leases like a car idling at a light. His mother had said, more than once, that a budget tells you the truth whether you like it or not, and he'd always heard it as one of those things adults say that sound wise and mean nothing. Now the numbers had actually turned on him, and the turning was the interesting part. Hazel Street wasn't better because it looked better. It was better because Pinecrest had a hidden requirement, and the requirement covered things Ryan hadn't even known needed covering. He owned a laptop, a bike, a thrift-store keyboard, and about four shirts. Was that worth insuring at all, if nobody made him?

He didn't know. That was the part that itched. At Hazel Street he could skip insurance entirely and keep his sixty dollars, but then a burst pipe or a break-in would be entirely his problem, his four shirts and his laptop floating away uninsured. At Pinecrest he'd be forced to carry the premium whether his stuff was worth it or not. One building trusted him to decide; the other didn't. Both, in their own bureaucratic ways, were telling him something about what he was responsible for, and he wasn't sure yet which version of himself he agreed with.

After class, in the parking lot, Lilly unlocked her bike and said, "So which one?"

"Hazel Street," Ryan said, then stopped. "Probably. Unless I think about the insurance thing more, in which case, ask me tomorrow."

"Decisive," Evan said.

"Shut up. I'm saving my decisiveness for the three-point turn." Ryan folded the two leases together, Hazel Street on the outside, and put them in his bag. "Did I pass today, Mr. Vu?"

Mr. Vu was already halfway to his ancient sedan. "You did not hit a single cone," he called back. "In this building, that is a triumph."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Signalling before a merge or lane change warns other drivers of the move; signalling too late, or not at all, gives them no time to adjust.
story:
The bus stop was two blocks from her house, and Katherine had walked there at 6:40 in the morning with the paper permit folded in her back pocket, the appointment for her road test stamped at the top. Ms. Bighorn was already on the bench, holding a canvas bag of groceries against her knees. She was the neighbour from four doors down, the one who waved from her porch but whose name Katherine had learned only last week, when the car lessons started and their street became a place where people watched each other drive.

"I failed mine twice," Ms. Bighorn said, without preamble. "Back when the tests were antiquated. They made you hill-park on a street with no hill."

Katherine laughed, but her hands were cold. She had passed the parallel parking at the practice cones yesterday, three times in a row, and still she kept seeing the rear tyre kiss the curb in her mind, the way it had on the first attempt, when she had cut the wheel too early and her mother, in the passenger seat, had gone very quiet. That silence had been worse than anything. Her mother did not criticize out loud; she withheld, and Katherine was left to impute the disappointment herself, to guess at its size.

"Test's on the highway?" Ms. Bighorn asked.

"Part of it. Two merges." Katherine said the word and felt the fear in it, specific and located, like a tooth. She had merged exactly once with her mother, on a Sunday, and it had gone wrong in a way she was still turning over. She had flicked the signal on as she was already steering into the lane, the lever and the wheel moving together, and the car behind had braked hard enough that she heard the tyres. Her mother had grabbed the dash and said only, "Katherine." Nothing else the whole drive home.

At the time she had decided her mother was being unfair, that the driver behind was tailgating, that the fault could be apportioned somewhere else. But she had lain awake doing the arithmetic of it anyway. The signal was supposed to come first. That was the entire point of it. If you flicked it on as you turned, or never flicked it at all, the other driver had no time to adjust, none, and the light became just a decoration on a move you'd already made. Signalling before the merge was what warned them, what gave them room to slow or shift or simply not die of surprise. She had done it backwards, announced a thing already in motion.

Rylie came around the corner then, earbuds in, pulling them out when she saw Katherine. "You're going now? My mom can't take you?"

"Bus. It's fine." Katherine had not wanted to owe Rylie's mother anything. Rylie had passed her test in March, on the second try, and had been gentle about it in a way that made Katherine feel twelve. "Did you fail yours for the merge thing?"

Rylie looked at the schedule board, then away. "Everyone in my family fails the merge the first time. It's like a tradition."

Katherine stared at her. Rylie had told everyone at school she'd failed on parallel parking. "You told Levi it was the parking."

"I told Levi a lot of things." Rylie shrugged, but her ears had gone red, and Katherine understood that the swagger had been armour, the same way her own quiet was, and that neither of them had ever said so. The bus was eleven minutes late. When it came, Ms. Bighorn stood, then paused with one hand on the pole.

"I proctor the road tests," she said. "Tuesdays and Thursdays. Not today, so you're safe from me." She smiled at Katherine's expression. "Small towns."

At the test centre, a woman with a clipboard slid into the passenger seat of her mother's car and said, "Head toward the on-ramp." Katherine pulled out, signalled, drove. When the ramp rose and the traffic came into view, she put the signal on early, a full stretch before the merge, and held it there, blinking, and watched the pickup truck behind ease off and make a gap. She slid into it. The woman wrote something on the clipboard. Three blocks later: "Pull over here and park between those two vehicles." Katherine looked at the space, checked her mirrors, signalled before she even began to slow, and started backing in, the wheel turning in her hands, the curb coming up in the side mirror like something rising through water.

"You're a touch crooked," the woman said. "Straighten it."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Kahlo painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera; they remarried the following year.
story:
The print of The Two Fridas had hung in her grandmother's hallway for as long as Maelle could remember, between the coat hooks and the door to the linen closet, so that a person hanging up a scarf had no choice but to stand beside it. Now she stood there on purpose, phone in hand, photographing it. Mr. Ndlovu had assigned each of them a painting to critique by Monday, formal analysis only: colour, composition, symbolism, no biography, no feelings dressed up as arguments. She had chosen the painting she knew best, which turned out to mean the painting she had never once looked at.

"Twelve minutes," her grandmother called from the kitchen, "and then you'll help me shell the peas."

Two women sat side by side on a bench, one in a white European dress, one in a Tehuana dress, their exposed hearts connected by a thin thread of blood. The stormy sky behind them took up more than half the canvas, Maelle noticed, finally, after sixteen years of walking past. The Frida in white held a small portrait in her hand and a pair of surgical scissors; the thread ran from the arm of that Frida to the heart of the other. The white dress bled onto the skirt in slow red dots, evenly spaced, almost decorative. She wrote in her notebook: complementary warm and cold values, red against white and blue. Then: symmetry, but broken. Then she stopped, because the third column, symbolism, was the one that mattered, and she did not know what the scissors meant.

Payton had been texting her all afternoon. Send me a pic of yours. I got a Monet, so jealous of anyone with a Kahlo. When Maelle sent the photograph, the reply came fast: omg the double self portrait?? She types two different lines of argument, Payton wrote, it's like two critiques of the same person. Maelle sat on the hallway floor with the phone on her knee and found she agreed, and that agreeing was not enough. Two perspectives was a nice phrase. Mr. Ndlovu would want to know which one the painting itself endorsed, if either, and how the colour made that argument, and where the composition placed the viewer, standing exactly where Maelle was standing, at the end of a hallway, unable to look away.

She helped shell the peas and asked her grandmother, the way you ask something casual when it is not casual, whether she knew anything about the painter.

"Her name was Frida Kahlo," her grandmother said, thumbing a pod open. "She painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera. They remarried the following year." She said it the way she recited the shipping forecast, matter-of-fact, and Maelle wrote nothing down because she was holding peas, and then wrote everything down the moment her hands were free.

The date undid her. She had been building a critique of a divided self, the loved Frida and the abandoned Frida, red and white, whole heart and cut heart, and it had seemed airtight. But 1939, the year of the divorce, meant the painting was made inside the wound, not after it, and the remarriage the following year meant the wound closed, or was agreed to close, which was different. The somatic detail of the scissors, the literal opened flesh, could be read as an ending or as an operation, and the painting refused to say which. She tried a new paragraph: the composition holds both women in one body of space, connected by thread, so that the painting's argument is not division but circulation. She crossed out circulation. Kept the thread.

At school on Monday, Payton leaned over her desk in Mr. Ndlovu's room. "I said Monet was about time," she whispered, "and he wrote 'good, now say how.'" When Maelle's turn came, she stood with her notes and gave the formal analysis straight: the cold dominance of the sky, the warm interruption of the blood, the bilateral symmetry that the left figure's bleeding arm quietly violates, the scissors as the one hard metallic note in a painting otherwise soft and organic. Then she said, "I read the date afterward, and it changed my reading. The year she divorced Rivera, and the remarriage the next year, mean the painting sits exactly between those two facts, and I can't decide whether the thread connecting the hearts is a lifeline or a tourniquet. I'm being honest that I can't decide. The painting may not want me to."

Mr. Ndlovu wrote something on his clipboard and did not say what. He only said, "Kiefer, you're next," and Maelle walked back to her seat past the window, where the light on the snow outside was doing something with white and grey that she caught herself, without meaning to, beginning to read.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Biotech billionaire Patrick Soon-Shiong bought the Los Angeles Times in 2018 for $500 million, plus the assumption of pension obligations.
story:
Sebastian had the living room to himself for most of the afternoon, which was the whole point of a Sunday. He sat on the floor with his back against the couch, a copy of the Los Angeles Times spread across the carpet like a savanna of gray columns, and he was halfway through a lugubrious piece about coastal erosion when his father came in carrying two mugs and sat down heavily in the armchair.

"Anything good," his father asked, though he asked it the way people ask about weather.

"There's a thing about the beaches washing away." Sebastian folded the page back. "Also the Rams lost, so, you know, a mixed day for the region."

His mother followed with her phone in her hand, screen glowing, and she did not sit so much as station herself near the window. "Dario's mother sent me that article," she said. "The one about the hospital deal. It ran three paragraphs. Three. And the developer bought a full page right beside it."

His father made a sound into his mug that was neither agreement nor dismissal.

"Wait," Sebastian said. "The paper ran a short story about something and then took money from the same people? Isn't that, like, the thing they always say they don't do?"

"It's complicated," his father said, in the tone of a man who had used the phrase often enough that it had worn smooth. "That paper was dying. Everybody knew it. Then in 2018 this biotech billionaire, Patrick Soon-Shiong, bought it for five hundred million dollars, and he took on the pension obligations too. All those workers, all those retired printers and editors. Somebody had to."

"And so he saved it," Sebastian said.

"And so he owns it," his mother said. "Those aren't the same sentence, even if they use the same words."

She held up her phone as though it were evidence in a trial Sebastian hadn't known he was attending. "You sequester the newsroom from the business side, on paper, and everyone signs the ethics policy, and then the owner plays golf with the developer. Nobody has to send a memo. The story just comes back three paragraphs long."

His father set the mug down. "You're describing a conspiracy."

"I'm describing gravity," she said. "Things fall toward money. You don't have to push them."

Sebastian looked from one to the other. He had grown up inside this exact argument, though usually it concerned the homeowners' association or his uncle's restaurant, and he knew the choreography: his mother suspicious, his father defending the reasonable middle, neither of them fully wrong. But the newspaper was different, because the newspaper was supposed to be the thing that told you who was wrong. He picked up the front section and turned it over, as if the truth might be printed on the back, which in a way it was: the subscriber services address, the corporate address, the small administrative print of a company that had to be owned by somebody.

He called Dario, who answered on the second ring with the sound of a basketball game behind him.

"Quick question," Sebastian said. "Who owns the paper you read?"

"My mom reads it, I read the box scores. Why, who died?"

"Nobody died. I need to know if it matters who owns a newspaper."

"Okay, weirdo. I guess it matters if they're, like, evil. My uncle says everything's owned by six guys, but my uncle also thinks the moon landing was staged in Nevada, so."

"That's not actually helpful."

"Want helpful? Ask Sunny. Her dad does something with media law, she won't shut up about it."

Sunny, when he texted her, sent back a voice note recorded over what sounded like a vacuum cleaner. "Two things," she said. "One, ownership isn't always the problem, sometimes it's the advertisers, sometimes it's just lazy editors, and you can't always tell which. Two, my dad says a paper with a rich owner is still better than no paper, and also worse than a paper nobody owns, and he says both sentences in the same breath, which is why my mom calls him a lawyer even at dinner."

Sebastian listened to it twice, sitting on the carpet among the scattered sections. His mother and father had drifted to the kitchen, and their voices came through the doorway in the low, unfinished way of a conversation that would resume at dinner and possibly for the next decade. What he had, he realized, was three people he trusted giving him accounts that overlapped without matching. His mother saw a hand on the scale. His father saw a rescue with strings. Sunny's father, distilled through a voice note, saw everything at once and refused to rank it.

He could hold both, he thought, and he could admit he couldn't yet weigh them. The paper on his floor had printed the erosion story and the short hospital story in the same morning, and he had read one and skipped the other, and that was a choice too, made by an owner he'd never heard of and a reader who hadn't checked.

At dinner he told them the Soon-Shiong fact straight, five hundred million plus the pensions, and watched his father nod and his mother narrow her eyes, and then he said, "I don't know which one of you is right."

"Good," his mother said, reaching for the bread. "That means you were paying attention to both of us."

His father raised his water glass a half inch, and Sebastian, after a moment, picked up his phone and typed a reminder to himself: find out who owns everything else I read.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is water-based while wet, but it dries quickly and becomes water-resistant once dry.
story:
Clara had promised herself she would finish the portrait before Sunday, and by Saturday afternoon it was almost there: her grandmother's face surfacing out of the canvas in layers of Payne's grey and warm ochre, the eyes still waiting for their last pass of white. She had left her brushes in a jar of water on the porch while she went inside to eat, and when she came back out forty minutes later, the water in the jar had gone cloudy and the brushes had gone hard. She picked one up and it felt like a small fossil in her hand, the bristles fused into a stiff, paint-crusted point.

She carried the jar to the outdoor faucet and ran the brushes under the stream, scrubbing them against her palm. The water slid off the dried paint without softening it. That was the thing she hadn't counted on, the thing Ms. Morningstar had mentioned only once, in passing, back in September when Clara had still been taking her class: while it's wet you can thin it with water, clean it with water, wash it right out of your clothes, but once it dries it stops caring about water altogether. Clara had filed it away as trivia and now she stood at the faucet learning it as a consequence.

Her grandmother had died in March, and Clara had volunteered to make the portrait for the memorial service without thinking very hard about what she was agreeing to. Her mother had eulogized the woman at the funeral, standing at the podium with two pages she never once looked down at, and afterward people kept telling Clara how much her mother's words had meant to them. Clara had sat in the second row and felt something she still couldn't name, something adjacent to jealousy, because she had a whole grandmother inside her too and no podium from which to say so. The painting was supposed to be her version of the speech.

Jayce came over at four, letting himself in through the side gate the way he always did, and found her on the porch with the ruined brushes laid out on a paper towel like evidence. "What happened to those?"

"I left them out." She turned the worst one over. "It dries fast. Faster than I thought. And then water does nothing, it just runs off."

"So they're dead?"

"Basically." She said it lightly, but she was thinking about the injunction she'd written to herself on a sticky note above her desk in April: finish it before the feeling fades. Her mother had told her that grief changes shape, and Clara had understood this to mean she should paint while the grief was still shaped like her grandmother's actual face. Six months later she wasn't sure that had been wisdom. Maybe the face she was painting was already a memory of a memory, softened at the edges like the one time she'd tried to draw her grandmother from a photograph and produced someone politer, more patient, less likely to tease her about her epicurean habits at the dinner table, reaching for the last of everything good.

Jayce sat down on the step and peered at the canvas. "That's really her," he said. "Like, exactly."

"Is it?" Clara looked at the eyes, the part she hadn't finished. "I keep thinking it's more like her at holidays. When she was performing."

"Maybe that's still her."

Ms. Morningstar appeared at the fence that divided the two yards, holding a colander of tomatoes she had no intention of giving away, only to display. "How's the great work?" she called. She was the kind of retired teacher who still assigned herself units of study, and she had taken an interest in the portrait from the beginning, asking about it each week with the fixed attention of someone keeping a student honest.

"Behind schedule," Clara said. "I ruined my good brushes."

Ms. Morningstar came as far as the porch rail and examined the jar. "Ah. You left them out." It wasn't a question, and it carried no lecture in it, only a small nod, as if Clara had confirmed something about the world that Ms. Morningstar had long since accepted. "You can soak them overnight, sometimes. Depends." She set a tomato on the railing anyway, a gift after all. "My mother painted in oils. Slowest medium on earth. She liked that about it. She said it gave her time to change her mind."

She went back inside, and Clara sat with that for a while. Acrylic was the opposite of slow, the opposite of time to change your mind; it dried on you while you hesitated, it committed you to the mark you'd already made. Her mother's eulogy had been like that too, written in a single night, delivered without revision, finished before anyone could argue with it. Clara had spent six months revising a face. She picked up the one brush that had survived, a cheap synthetic one she'd been too lazy to wash properly but which still had some flex left in it, and squeezed out a nickel of titanium white.

"Are you going to do the eyes now?" Jayce asked.

"In a minute." She wet the brush in clean water and thinned the paint until it moved the way she wanted, thinking that this was the part she liked, the brief window when the paint was still hers to dilute and direct, still obedient. Once it dried it would belong to the canvas. "I'm deciding something first."

"Which is?"

"Whether the eyes should look at whoever's standing in front of it, or off to the side. Like she's watching something in the room."

Jayce considered the canvas from the porch step, chin on his knees. "What was she usually watching?"

Clara laughed, a short sound that surprised her. "The food. Everybody's plates. Whether you'd actually eaten." She touched the loaded brush to the edge of the palette, taking off the excess. Then she leaned in and laid the first small crescent of white along the lower lid of the left eye, working fast, before it could set on her.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the youngest child able to do so traditionally asks the Four Questions, which begin 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
Xavier had run the Seder exactly eleven times in his head by Thursday afternoon, and in all eleven versions everything went perfectly, which should have been his first warning. His grandmother had done it every year until last spring, and now his mother had looked at him across the kitchen and said, "You know it best," and he had said yes before he had fully decided anything. That was the kind of thing he did. He said yes and then worked backward to find the reasons.

He sat at the cleared dining table with the Haggadahs stacked in front of him, the good ones with the cracked spines, and walked himself through the order. Kadesh, then the washing, then the vegetable. He had it. Of course he had it. Anyone paying even mild attention since the age of six would have it, and Xavier had been paying fanatical attention, the way he paid attention to everything, which people sometimes malign as showing off when really it was closer to fear.

His little brother wandered in with a juice box and stood at the edge of the table, watching. Xavier called him over and turned to the right page. "Okay. You're doing the Four Questions this year." His brother stared at the juice box. "I forget how it starts." Xavier tapped the line. "Why is this night different from all other nights? That's the first one. You ask all four, in order, and I answer them later, that's the whole deal. Youngest kid who can manage it asks, and that's you now." His brother said the opening phrase once, quietly, testing it, and Xavier felt something in his chest unclench slightly, because if the kid could ask, then Xavier could answer, and the night would hold its shape.

Desiree called him that evening while he was portioning out the charoset into the good dish. She had been to their Seder two years ago, dragged along by a mutual friend, and she still remembered the horseradish, which she described with grudging respect. "So you're running it," she said. "Postulate: you will make everyone cry by the third cup of wine." "That's not what postulate means and it's not a goal." "It could be both." He laughed, which he had not done all day, and after she hung up he caught himself rehearsing the laugh, the exact way it had gone, as though he could save it for later and use it at the table when things got stiff.

Friday he dragged his brother into the living room for a full rehearsal, and his brother turned out to be obstreperous about it, flopping sideways on the couch, singing the Four Questions to a tune he was inventing on the spot, asking whether he could do them in a robot voice. Xavier felt the familiar heat in his ears, the one that made him want to take the whole thing back and do every part himself, including the questions, which he could obviously deliver better than a ten-year-old. He was absolutely certain of that. He was, in fact, so certain that he had already drafted a backup plan in which he performed both halves of the dialogue himself, a plan he had told no one because some part of him knew how it would sound.

Instead he sat down on the couch next to his brother and said, "Robot voice is fine." His brother did the whole set as a robot, halting and tuneless, and somewhere in the second question, the one about why we eat bitter herbs, the robot voice dropped away and it was just his brother's voice, small and careful, getting every word right. Xavier did not correct anything. He noticed this about himself the way you notice you have been holding your breath.

The Seder itself did not go the way any of his eleven mental versions had gone. The soup was late, an uncle argued about politics until Xavier steered him back with a line his grandmother used to use, and the wine glass for Elijah got set at the wrong place and moved twice. But when the moment came, his brother stood up, put one hand flat on the table like a tiny lawyer, and asked why this night was different from all other nights, and the room went quiet in the old way, the way Xavier remembered from before last spring. He answered from the book, mostly. Once or twice he answered from somewhere else, some memory of how his grandmother had phrased it, and whether that memory was accurate he honestly could not say. He had been telling himself all week that he knew exactly what he was doing, and the truest thing was that he knew most of it and borrowed the rest.

Afterward, in the kitchen, washing the good dish, he found his mother leaning against the counter watching him. "You let him do the robot voice," she said. "Grandma would have died." "She would have laughed first," Xavier said, and his mother considered this, and did not argue, and handed him the towel.
